strengths: Addresses critical gap in literature: establishes direct evaluation benchmark for MLH (energies/forces), revealing that prior work focused only on reconstruction metrics. This is methodologically important for the field.

Technically sound: rigorous treatment of SO(3) equivariance, proper implementation of Kohn-Sham energy/force evaluation, careful handling of non-self-consistency with detailed theoretical and empirical analysis (Section G.8).

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple datasets (MD17, rMD17 with recomputed labels, QH9), fair comparisons with re-trained MLIP baselines, extensive ablations (Tables 10-14), scaling studies, and deep analyses (geometry optimization, Hessians, frontier orbitals, MO-basis error decomposition).
Strong empirical results: 40% lower Hamiltonian error than prior MLH with half the parameters; first MLH reaching NequIP-level force accuracy on MD17; 20× better energy errors on QH9 vs MACE.

Valuable theoretical insights: perturbative explanation showing energy errors scale as O(||δH||²) while forces scale as O(||δH||), explaining energy-force gap. MO-basis error analysis (Table 24) shows virtual-virtual errors don't affect energy to first order, explaining why global Hamiltonian MAE is misleading.
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters (Tables 6-8), promised code release, rMD17 recomputation with consistent DFT settings, clear experimental documentation.
Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges non-self-consistent forces, fixed basis/functional, closed-shell only, computational cost. These are discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Limited practical advantage for primary use case: NequIP already matches force accuracy (~0.93 meV/Å on MD17) and is 20× faster (0.167s vs 1.56s per structure). The Fock build dominates computational cost (~1.5s), not model inference. Main MLH advantage (orbital access) is not demonstrated to solve real problems in the tested applications (MD trajectories).

Scalability limitations: all benchmarks on small molecules (≤21 atoms); zero-shot transfer to larger molecules (45-98 atoms) shows degradation beyond 80 atoms (energy MAE >1 eV/atom, Table 21); closed-shell systems only; no OMol25-scale evaluation.

Initialization dependence: Table 13 shows catastrophic performance loss without MinAO initialization (energy error increases ~20×), suggesting model partially memorizes initialization. Raises concerns about transfer to different basis sets/DFT settings but not adequately discussed.

Heavy reliance on concurrent work: SO(2) backbone from eSEN (Fu et al., 2025), flow matching from Kim et al. (2025), tensor expansion from QHNet (Yu et al., 2023b). Paper primarily combines existing techniques rather than introducing fundamentally novel methods.

Experimental fairness concerns: QH9 MLIP comparisons use published QM9 results rather than retraining on identical splits; HELM and QHNetV2 codebases not publicly available limiting direct validation; eSEN comparison (most relevant baseline) relegated to appendix.

Non-self-consistent forces: while analyzed in detail, using forces from non-self-consistent densities has conceptual limitations. Forces after SCF convergence would be more principled, though Table 23 shows discrepancy is comparable to DFT artifacts.

Limited generalization study: only tested within PBE/def2-SVP or B3LYP/def2-SVP; no cross-functional transfer (train on PBE, test on B3LYP); severely limits applicability for practitioners needing flexibility across DFT settings.
Missing key ablation: no comparison of Hamiltonian prediction vs. direct E/F training with identical architecture. Cannot quantify structural advantage of predicting H vs. just regressing E/F.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MD17, rMD17, QH9, ∇2DFT) with extensive ablations and supplementary analyses
Addresses a genuine gap by evaluating Hamiltonians via direct downstream energy-force computation rather than just reconstruction metrics
Sound technical approach combining SO(2)-equivariant backbone with two-stage pair refinement, supported by thorough ablations (Tables 10-14)
Establishes rMD17 benchmark with recomputed Hamiltonians, providing a valuable resource for future work
Insightful perturbative analysis explaining energy-force accuracy gap (Section G.8), with empirical validation of scaling relationships
weaknesses: Unclear practical utility: paper fails to establish compelling use case over existing methods. End-to-end computational cost dominated by PySCF (~0.5-0.9s per geometry, Table 18) overwhelms inference speedup, and SCF acceleration is only 2.18×
Severe scalability failure beyond ~80 atoms: energy MAE exceeds 1 eV/atom and SCF cycles exceed 100%, meaning predicted Hamiltonians slow down convergence (Table 21)

Critical dependence on initial Hamiltonian: Without MinAO initialization, Hamiltonian MAE degrades from 9.18→25.50 µEh (Table 13), suggesting model learns residual correction rather than true Hamiltonian prediction
Fixed DFT settings (PBE/def2-SVP or B3LYP/def2-SVP) severely restrict applicability; transfer across functionals and basis sets not demonstrated despite being listed as key limitation

Energy-force asymmetry suggests model doesn't learn physical Hamiltonian: forces remain comparable to MLIPs despite superior energy accuracy, indicating fundamentally different solution to energy vs. force prediction

Unfair MLIP comparisons: total end-to-end time including PySCF post-processing often exceeds MLIP inference, yet accuracy advantages are marginal for forces; no total wall-clock comparison in main text
Non-self-consistent force evaluation is non-standard; analytic forces from predicted densities may not reflect proper DFT behavior and generalize poorly to production simulations
Limited generalization: only organic molecules (C,H,N,O,F), single basis set, narrow chemical diversity; zero-shot transfer to larger molecules fails completely

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in literature: identifies that prior MLH work was evaluated mainly on reconstruction metrics rather than direct downstream accuracy (energies/forces), and proposes comprehensive benchmark to rectify this
Thorough experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (MD17, rMD17, QH9, ∇2DFT, PubChemQH) with proper ablations demonstrating each design choice's importance

Solid technical contributions: two-stage pair update improves off-diagonal Hamiltonian accuracy and robustness; SO(2) backbone improves parameter efficiency (40% error reduction with 50% fewer parameters)
Rigorous methodology: consistent evaluation pipeline using PySCF, recomputed rMD17 for benchmark consistency, proper handling of non-self-consistent forces with theoretical and empirical analysis

Exceptional depth of analysis: perturbative explanation of energy-force gaps validated empirically (Table 22); MO-basis decomposition explaining why virtual-space errors don't affect ground state energies; geometry optimization validation showing QHFlow2 better reproduces local PES than NequIP

Demonstrates tangible practical value: first MLH model reaching NequIP-level force accuracy; 2.18× SCF speedup shown in controlled setting; provides access to electronic structure (orbitals, density, frontier orbitals) unavailable to MLIPs

Honest limitations discussion and reproducibility: acknowledges scope restrictions (fixed DFT settings, closed-shell only, one-shot forces), provides extensive experimental details, promises code release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: two-stage pair update combines existing ideas (SO(2), tensor products) without fundamentally new concepts; flow matching is straightforward application of existing technique; architecture largely assembles prior work (eSEN backbone, QHNet tensor expansion)

Severe practical limitations: computational cost dominated by DFT evaluation (Table 18 shows QHFlow2 10-100× slower than MLIPs); only advantage is electronic structure access, which isn't always needed; energy/force evaluation requires full Fock build per prediction

Restrictive experimental scope: limited to fixed DFT settings (PBE/def2-SVP for MD17, B3LYP/def2-SVP for QH9) with no transfer studies to other functionals/bases; closed-shell systems only; one-shot non-self-consistent force evaluation; zero-shot generalization degrades beyond ~80 atoms (Table 21)

Energy-force accuracy gap: substantial gap between energy and force MAE across all models (e.g., Figure 2: ~0.003 meV energy but ~0.34 meV/Å forces for QHFlow2-m) limits practical MD utility; while theoretically explained, practically concerning

Incomplete baseline comparisons: HELM and QHNetV2 codebases unavailable for fair comparison; most MLIP comparisons use published results on different splits rather than matched experimental setup; some recent work comparisons limited

Statistical rigor concerns: no error bars or confidence intervals reported; single runs for most experiments; GPU kernel non-determinism mentioned but not quantified; claims like 'first to reach NequIP-level force accuracy' require careful reading to parse correctly

Presentation density: extensive appendices required for full understanding; key architectural comparisons (eSEN vs QHNetV2) relegated to appendix D.3; some design decisions not well-justified (e.g., why two-stage update specifically)
